finding.claim: Unauthenticated SQL injection in /search: the q query parameter is interpolated into an f-string SQL LIKE clause, so an attacker can break out of the string literal and run UNION-based queries to read any table in shop.db.
finding.source: app.py:11 request.args.get("q", "") (GET /search?q=...), no auth guard on the route
finding.sink: app.py:12 db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'")

trace.note: Route /search is registered with no auth decorator or middleware in this file
term is read from the query string, default empty string, no validation
term is concatenated into SQL text inside a single-quoted LIKE literal; a quote in term closes the literal
Result rows are returned as JSON, so UNION-injected columns are disclosed to the attacker in the response

finding.guards_checked: No parameter binding on this query (unlike /product and /by-owner); no escaping, allowlist, or length limit; no upstream framework sanitization visible in app.py. sqlite3 execute() rejects stacked statements, but UNION-based extraction still works. Example payload: q=%' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master--

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:9 is a bare @app.route("/search") with no auth decorator, so the attacker is anonymous. app.py:11 reads q with no validation or allowlist. app.py:12 interpolates it into the SQL text with an f-string and no parameter binding; the parameterized /product (app.py:18) and /by-owner (app.py:25) routes do not apply here. app.py:13 returns the rows as JSON, so UNION-injected columns are disclosed. sqlite3's single-statement restriction does not block UNION extraction.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous and reaches app.py:12, where the unparameterized f-string puts the q value from app.py:11 into the SQL text with no escaping, allowlist, or auth check, so a payload such as `%' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master--` breaks out of the LIKE literal and the results come back in the app.py:13 response.
